items.stem: Which statement about the types of wave is correct?

options.text: A wave may be either transverse or longitudinal.
Every wave is transverse, as the diagrams show.
The type depends on how the wave gets drawn.
Water waves are the only transverse waves.

items.why: The specification states that waves may be either transverse or longitudinal, so both types exist.

items.stem: A sound wave travels through air. What is a rarefaction in this wave?

options.text: A region where the air particles are pushed together.
A region where the air particles move across the wave.
A region where the air particles are further apart.
A region of empty space with no air particles.

items.why: A rarefaction is where the particles of the medium are spread out, giving a lower pressure than normal.

items.stem: Which statement about a sound wave travelling through air is correct?

options.text: It is transverse, because it is displayed as a wavy trace.
It is longitudinal, so it must have a solid to travel through.
It is transverse, with crests and troughs of moving air.
It is longitudinal, with compressions and rarefactions.

items.why: Sound waves travelling through air are longitudinal, and longitudinal waves show areas of compression and rarefaction.

items.stem: Ripples on a water surface are an example of a transverse wave. Why?

options.text: The water surface oscillates back and forth along the direction the ripple travels.
The water surface oscillates up and down, across the direction the ripple moves.
The water is carried forwards across the pond as every ripple passes it.
The ripple is always drawn as a curved line in the textbook diagrams.

items.why: In a transverse wave the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer, which is what the surface does.

items.stem: What is the difference between a longitudinal wave and a transverse wave?

options.text: A longitudinal wave carries the material of the medium along with it, while a transverse wave carries only the energy.
In a longitudinal wave the oscillations are parallel to the direction of travel, and in a transverse wave they are perpendicular to it.
In a longitudinal wave the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of travel, and in a transverse wave they are parallel.
A longitudinal wave is drawn as a row of straight lines, while a transverse wave is always drawn as a wavy curve.

items.why: This is the defining difference: the two types are separated by the direction of the oscillations relative to the direction of travel.

items.stem: One end of a long slinky is pushed and pulled repeatedly along its length. Which description of the wave produced is correct?

options.text: Longitudinal, because the coils vibrate along the direction the wave travels.
Transverse, because the coils vibrate across the direction that the wave travels.
Longitudinal, because the coils are carried along to the far end of it.
Transverse, because a moving bunch of coils is seen along the slinky.

items.why: Pushing and pulling along the slinky makes the coils oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer, giving compressions and rarefactions.

items.stem: A ball floats on a still pond while ripples pass beneath it. Which observation is evidence that the water itself does not travel?

options.text: The ball is carried away to the far bank by ripples.
The ball edges a little further forwards as each ripple passes.
The far side of the pond becomes deeper as the ripples arrive.
The ball bobs up and down but stays in the same place.

items.why: The float returns to its position after every ripple, showing that the wave passes through the water while the water stays put.

items.stem: A loudspeaker plays loud music. Which observation is evidence that the air itself does not travel across the room to the listener?

options.text: A steady breeze can be felt coming from the loudspeaker cone.
A candle flame placed in front of the loudspeaker is blown out.
No draught is felt by the listener as the music plays.
The music is heard a moment after the cone starts moving.

items.why: If air travelled across the room there would be a draught. The air only oscillates and passes the disturbance on.

items.stem: A transverse wave is drawn with its undisturbed position shown as a horizontal centre line. What is the amplitude of this wave?

options.text: The maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed position
The vertical distance from the bottom of a trough up to the top of a crest
The displacement of a point on the wave at the instant it is measured
The distance a point on the wave travels while one whole wave passes

items.why: The specification definition: amplitude is measured from the undisturbed line to a crest or trough.

items.stem: Which distance on a wave diagram is exactly one wavelength?

options.text: From the first crest drawn on the diagram to the very last crest drawn
From a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave
From the top of a crest to the bottom of the trough next to it
From the centre line up to the top of the crest above it

items.why: The specification definition; crest to the next crest is the usual example of it.

items.stem: What does the frequency of a wave tell you?

options.text: The speed at which a wave moves through the medium
The number of complete waves drawn on the diagram
The number of waves passing a point each second
The time taken for one wave to pass a point

items.why: The specification definition of frequency.

items.stem: Ripples pass a floating cork. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The frequency is the speed at which the ripples travel
The amplitude is the cork's displacement at any instant
The wavelength is the gap from a crest to the next trough
The period is the time one whole ripple takes to pass

items.why: The period is the time taken for one complete wave to pass a point.

items.stem: Which statement about the period of a wave is correct?

options.text: It is measured in hertz, the same unit as the frequency
It is measured in waves per second, like the frequency
It is measured in metres, like the wavelength
It is measured in seconds, because it is a time

items.why: The specification gives period, T, in seconds, s.

items.stem: What is meant by the wave speed?

options.text: The speed at which particles of the medium move up and down
The number of complete waves that pass a point each second
The speed at which the energy is transferred through the medium
The speed at which the source producing the wave vibrates

items.why: The specification defines wave speed as the speed at which the energy is transferred, or the wave moves, through the medium.

items.stem: Which statement about the wave equation is correct?

options.text: It applies only to transverse waves, such as water ripples
It applies to light waves but not to sound waves
It applies only to waves whose speed stays constant
It applies to all waves, transverse and longitudinal

items.why: The specification states that all waves obey the wave equation.

items.stem: How is the wave speed related to the frequency and the wavelength?

options.text: The wave speed is the frequency times the wavelength
The wave speed is the frequency divided by the wavelength
The wave speed is the frequency added to the wavelength
The wave speed is the amplitude times the frequency

items.why: wave speed = frequency × wavelength, the equation as the specification states it.

items.stem: A student uses [v = f λ] with the frequency in hertz and the wavelength in metres. What unit does the calculated wave speed have?

options.text: Hertz, Hz, the unit taken from the frequency
Metres, m, the unit taken from the wavelength
Seconds, s, because speed always involves a time
Metres per second, m/s, since the answer is a speed

items.why: The specification gives wave speed, v, in metres per second, m/s.

items.stem: A wave has a frequency of 8 Hz. What is its period?

options.text: 8 s

items.why: period = (1)/(frequency) = 1/8 = 0.125 s.

items.stem: A wave has a period of 0.004 s. Using [T = 1/f], what is its frequency?

options.text: 25 Hz
4 Hz
250 Hz

items.stem: In one second, 400 complete waves pass a point. How should this be recorded?

options.text: 400 Hz, because 400 waves pass each second
400 s, because the waves are counted over a second
0.0025 Hz, because frequency is one over 400
400 m/s, because the waves move past the point

items.why: The specification gives frequency, f, in hertz, Hz, and 1 Hz is one wave each second.

items.stem: The wave equation is [v = f λ]. Which rearrangement correctly gives the wavelength?

options.text: λ = f / v, the frequency divided by the wave speed
λ = v / f, the speed divided by the frequency
λ = v f, the speed multiplied by the frequency
λ = v − f, subtracting the frequency from the speed

items.why: Dividing both sides of v = f λ by f gives λ = v/f.

items.stem: A sound wave has a frequency of 2.5 kHz. What is this frequency in hertz?

options.text: 250 Hz
25 Hz

items.stem: Ripples on a tank have a wavelength of 40 cm and a frequency of 5 Hz. What is their wave speed?

options.text: 2 m/s
2 m

items.stem: A wave is shown on a graph of displacement against distance. How are the amplitude and the wavelength read from it?

options.text: Amplitude runs from a trough up to the crest above it
Both are measured along the horizontal distance axis
Amplitude is vertical, wavelength is horizontal
Wavelength runs from one crest to the next trough

items.why: Amplitude is read up the displacement axis, wavelength along the distance axis.

items.stem: A class measures the speed of sound in air. Which method gives the most reliable value?

options.text: Time the echo of a clap from a wall a measured distance away
Measure how loud the clap is at two different distances
Use a stopwatch to time a clap crossing the laboratory
Ask two students to clap together and time the delay

items.why: A long path gives a time large enough for reaction time to matter little; speed = (2 × distance) ÷ time.

items.stem: In the echo method for the speed of sound, the distance to the wall is measured but twice that distance is used in the calculation. Why?

options.text: Because the sound must spread out in every direction from the clap
Because the wall creates a new wave that travels more slowly
Because the sound travels to the wall and back before it is heard
Because sound travels faster on its way back from the wall

items.why: The timed interval covers two equal journeys, so the path is 2 × the distance to the wall.

items.stem: Which is a suitable method for measuring the speed of ripples on a water surface?

options.text: Count the ripples reaching the far edge and multiply by the depth
Use the dipper frequency and a measured wavelength in v = f λ
Measure the height of the ripples and divide it by the frequency
Time one ripple with a stopwatch over a two centimetre gap

items.why: Frequency is read from the signal generator and wavelength from the projected pattern.

items.stem: Why is a stroboscope or a video recording often used when ripples are studied in a ripple tank?

options.text: It increases the frequency of the ripples on the water surface
A stopwatch would time the ripples just as well
It makes the ripples taller so the amplitude can be measured
It freezes the pattern so wavelengths can be measured

items.why: A still pattern lets a ruler be laid across ten wavelengths on the projected image.

items.stem: In required practical activity 8, which apparatus is most suitable for measuring the wavelength of ripples in a ripple tank?

options.text: A ruler measuring across just one ripple
A ruler measuring the height of a single ripple crest
A stopwatch timing one ripple crossing the tank
A ruler placed under the projected ripple pattern

items.why: The projected pattern is still enough to measure across, ideally over ten wavelengths.

items.stem: (Physics only) A sound wave passes from air into water, where it travels faster. What happens to its frequency and its wavelength?

options.text: The wavelength stays the same and the frequency increases
Both the frequency and the wavelength become larger
The frequency stays the same and the wavelength becomes longer
The frequency stays the same and the wavelength gets shorter

items.why: With f fixed and v larger, v = f λ requires λ to increase in the same proportion.

items.stem: (Physics only) Sound travels faster in a steel rail than in air. When a sound passes from the air into the steel, which quantity is fixed by the source and cannot change?

options.text: The frequency, which is set by the vibrating source
The wave speed, which depends on the source's energy
The wavelength, because the wave keeps its shape
The period, which grows longer in the steel

items.why: The source sends the same number of waves each second whatever medium receives them.

items.stem: In required practical activity 8, waves are also sent along a stretched string. Why is the distance across ten wavelengths measured and then divided by ten?

options.text: The wavelength changes as the wave crosses the whole string
It reduces the effect of uncertainty in each reading
Measuring one wavelength alone would give the same result
Ten readings must be taken in every school experiment

items.why: The same ruler uncertainty is a much smaller fraction of a ten-times-longer distance.

items.stem: A sound wave travelling through the air reaches a thick concrete wall. Which statement best describes reflection at this boundary?

options.text: Some of the sound is sent back into the air it originally came from
Reflection cannot occur here, as concrete is not polished
All of the sound must pass on into the concrete and travel through
The wall turns the sound into a wave of a much higher frequency

items.why: Reflection at a boundary sends part of the wave back into the first material, and air and concrete are two different materials.

items.stem: A radio wave meets a thick metal sheet and is absorbed. What happens to the energy that the wave was carrying?

options.text: It is destroyed, so less energy exists than there was before
It is transferred to the thermal energy store of the metal
It is stored inside the wave until that wave is set free again
It becomes a reflected wave of exactly the same frequency

items.why: Absorption transfers the energy carried by the wave into the energy stores of the material, most often the thermal store.

items.stem: Light from a street lamp shines on a clean window and carries on into the room beyond. Which word describes what the light has done at the glass?

options.text: The light has been absorbed by glass
The light has been reflected away
The light has been fully destroyed
The light has been transmitted

items.why: Transmission is a wave passing through the boundary and continuing to travel inside the second material.

items.stem: You are drawing a ray diagram for light reflecting from a plane mirror. From which line is the angle of incidence measured?

options.text: From the normal, drawn at right angles to the mirror surface
From the mirror surface, at the point where the ray lands on it
From the flat surface, along where the ray hits it
From the bottom edge of the paper the diagram sits on

items.why: Angles of incidence and reflection are always measured between the ray and the normal at the point of incidence.

items.stem: Which feature must appear in a correctly drawn ray diagram showing reflection at a plane mirror?

options.text: A dashed normal drawn along the mirror surface
Arrows on the rays to show the direction
The image marked in front of the mirror surface
An angle of reflection larger than incidence

items.why: Rays are drawn as straight lines carrying arrows, so the diagram shows which way the light is travelling.

items.stem: A lamp lights a plane mirror and a sheet of white paper equally. A clear image is seen in the mirror but not in the paper. Why is this?

options.text: The rough paper scatters rays and so breaks the law of reflection
The paper absorbs every ray of light that arrives at it
The smooth mirror keeps parallel rays parallel when they reflect
Paper transmits light, but a mirror is unable to transmit

items.why: Specular reflection at a smooth surface preserves the pattern of the rays so an image forms, whereas the rough paper scatters them.

items.stem: A narrow ray of light travels through air and meets the flat surface of a glass block. Which statement about this boundary is correct?

options.text: All the light is transmitted, because the glass is transparent
All the light is absorbed, since the glass warms up a little
Some light is transmitted into the glass and some is reflected back
None of the light gets in until the angle reaches ninety degrees

items.why: In general all three effects occur together, and a faint reflected ray is visible alongside the much brighter transmitted one.

items.stem: A ray strikes a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of 30°. What is the angle of reflection, and from where is it measured?

options.text: 60°, measured from the normal, since they total 90°
30°, measured from the surface of the mirror
60°, measured from the mirror surface, not the normal
30°, measured from the normal on its other side

items.why: The law of reflection gives angle of reflection = angle of incidence, with both angles measured from the normal.

items.stem: A matt black metal plate and a shiny silver metal plate are left side by side in bright sunlight. Why does the black plate become hotter?

options.text: It reflects more of the light, and reflection is what warms a surface
The silver plate reflects all the light, so it absorbs none and cannot warm up
The silver plate absorbs the light but re-emits all of it at once
It absorbs more of the light, transferring that energy to its thermal store

items.why: Absorption at the interface transfers the energy of the wave into the material and raises its temperature; reflected energy leaves again.

items.stem: Heavy fabric curtains are drawn across a window facing a busy road, and the room becomes noticeably quieter. Which effect best explains this?

options.text: The curtain reflects all the sound waves straight back
The soft fabric absorbs much of the sound that reaches it
The curtain bounces the noise straight back outdoors
The curtain slows the sound so it arrives too late to hear

items.why: Soft porous materials absorb sound, transferring the energy of the wave to their thermal energy store, so less is transmitted into the room.

items.stem: In Required practical activity 9 a ray of light is shone from air into a rectangular glass block, meeting the surface at an angle to the normal. What is seen as the ray enters the block?

options.text: It bends away from the normal
It carries straight on, unbent
It bends towards the normal
It spreads out and bends away from the normal

items.why: Light slows on entering glass, so a ray meeting the surface at an angle to the normal is refracted towards the normal.

items.stem: In Required practical activity 9 a ray box is aimed at a plane mirror, then at gloss card, then at matt card. Which quantity must be kept the same throughout?

options.text: The angle of incidence of the ray from the box
The kind of surface that the ray box is aimed at
The surface type placed in front of the ray box
The sharpness of the reflected ray on paper

items.why: The type of surface is the independent variable, so the angle of incidence is the control variable and must be held constant.

items.stem: A hammer strikes one end of a long steel rail. A student with an ear pressed against the far end hears the blow. What is happening inside the steel as the sound travels along it?

options.text: Particles of the steel vibrate about their positions and pass the disturbance on
Sound slips along the tiny gaps of air trapped between the steel particles
Sound leaves the rail at once and reaches the ear through the air
The rail as a whole slides towards the listener as the wave passes

items.why: Sound waves can travel through solids causing vibrations in the solid: each particle vibrates and hands the disturbance to its neighbour.

items.stem: A sound wave travelling through the air arrives at a person's ear. Which statement describes how this leads to the sensation of sound?

options.text: The ear drum turns the wave straight into electricity and never moves
The wave passes on unchanged along the ear canal and into the brain
The wave makes the ear drum and other parts of the ear vibrate
The ear amplifies the wave until it is loud enough to hear

items.why: Within the ear, sound waves cause the ear drum and other parts to vibrate, which causes the sensation of sound.

items.stem: What is the range of normal human hearing?

options.text: from 20 Hz to 200 kHz
from 20 Hz to 20 kHz
from 2 Hz to 20 000 Hz
from 20 Hz up to 2000 Hz

items.why: Students should know that the range of normal human hearing is from 20 Hz to 20 kHz.

items.stem: A bat call at 45 kHz is played to a class through an ultrasonic transducer at very high intensity. Nobody in the room hears anything. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The sound is far too quiet by the time that it has reached anybody's ear
A 45 kHz pressure wave in air is not a sound wave, so there is nothing to hear
Only very high frequencies are lost, and hearing them can be trained back
The ear cannot convert a wave of that frequency into vibrations

items.why: The conversion of sound waves to vibrations of solids works over a limited frequency range, and this restricts the limits of human hearing.

items.stem: Explain why the process by which the ear detects sound works only over a limited frequency range, and what this means for what a person can hear.

options.text: Sound waves outside a limited band cannot be converted into vibrations of the ear's solid parts
Outside that band no sound wave exists at all, so there is simply nothing arriving at the ear to detect
The brain selects the frequencies it accepts, so the ear itself passes on every sound wave arriving
The quietest sounds go first, so the range narrows whenever the wave becomes less intense

items.why: The conversion of sound waves to vibrations of solids works over a limited frequency range, and this restricts the limits of human hearing.

items.stem: Music from a loudspeaker in one room can be heard through a solid brick wall in the room next door. Which statement best describes the part the wall plays?

options.text: It blocks the sound entirely, so what is heard has leaked round the edges
The brick itself vibrates and carries the sound wave to the far side
Sound seeps through the pores of trapped air inside the brick
It reflects the whole wave, so only an echo is heard nearby

items.why: Sound waves can travel through solids causing vibrations in the solid; the vibrating brick then radiates sound into the second room.

items.stem: A singer's voice is picked up by a microphone and played back through a loudspeaker. Which statement correctly describes what happens at the microphone diaphragm and at the loudspeaker cone?

options.text: Both the diaphragm and the cone turn a sound wave into vibrations of a solid
The diaphragm vibrates the air, while the cone stops the air vibrating
Sound waves set the diaphragm vibrating, and the vibrating cone makes sound waves
Neither part is a solid vibrating, so no conversion of the wave can occur

items.why: The conversion runs between sound waves and vibrations in solids in both directions, which is exactly what a microphone and a loudspeaker do.

items.stem: A drum is struck in a hall and a listener standing a few metres away in the air hears the beat. Which sequence of events describes what happens?

options.text: Air vibrates first, then the drum skin vibrates, and then the beat is heard
The sound squeezes through tiny air gaps in the floor to get to the listener
The drum skin vibrates and the sound wave itself travels to the brain
The skin vibrates, a sound wave crosses the air, and the ear drum vibrates

items.why: A vibrating solid generates the sound wave, and the wave then converts back into vibrations of a solid at the ear drum.

items.stem: Which statement about ultrasound waves is correct?

options.text: Their frequency is below the lowest frequency a person hears
They are electromagnetic waves, like the X-rays used in hospitals
They are ordinary sound waves that are simply far too quiet to hear
Their frequency is above the highest frequency a person hears

items.why: The specification states that ultrasound waves have a frequency higher than the upper limit of hearing for humans. They remain sound waves in every other respect.

items.stem: Which statement about P-waves and S-waves is correct?

options.text: P-waves are transverse and S-waves are longitudinal
Both P-waves and S-waves are longitudinal waves
P-waves are longitudinal, S-waves transverse
Both P-waves and S-waves are transverse waves

items.why: The specification states that P-waves are longitudinal, seismic waves and S-waves are transverse, seismic waves. It is the transverse S-wave that cannot travel through a liquid.

items.stem: A survey team sends waves down into the ground to look for a buried rock layer in which the waves would travel at a different speed. What happens when the waves reach the top of that buried layer?

options.text: The waves carry on downwards at exactly the same speed
Part of each wave is reflected back and the rest travels on
All of each wave is reflected and none of it travels on
The waves are all absorbed at the top of the buried layer

items.why: A change of velocity at a boundary between two different media produces a partial reflection. The reflected part returns to the detector and reveals the layer; the transmitted part carries on and can reflect from deeper boundaries.

items.stem: An ultrasound pulse travelling through soft tissue meets a boundary with bone. What happens to the pulse at that boundary?

options.text: All of it bounces back and none enters the bone
None of it comes back; it all enters the bone
Part of it is reflected, part carries on
It is absorbed there and turned into heat

items.why: The specification says ultrasound waves are partially reflected when they meet a boundary between two different media. The reflected part times that boundary; the rest travels on to the next one.

items.stem: An ultrasound pulse leaves a probe on a patient's skin and travels at 1500 m/s. The reflection from a boundary inside the body is detected 0.001 s after the pulse leaves the probe. How far is that boundary from the probe?

options.text: 3 m

items.why: Distance travelled = speed × time = 1500 × 0.001 = 1.5 m. That is the there-and-back path, so the boundary is half of it away: 0.75 m.

items.stem: A ship measures water depth by echo sounding. It records the time between sending a sound pulse downwards and detecting the echo. How is the depth found from that time?

options.text: Multiply the time by the speed of sound in water
Divide the speed of sound in water by that time
Halve the time, multiply by the speed, halve again
Multiply the time by the speed of sound, then halve it

items.why: Speed × time gives the whole path the pulse travelled, down to the sea bed and back. The depth is half of that. Halving the time first and then multiplying would be equally correct.

items.stem: After an earthquake, detectors on the far side of the Earth record P-waves but no S-waves. What does this indicate about the Earth's core?

options.text: No seismic wave of any kind can pass through the core
There is an empty gap inside the Earth stopping the S-waves
S-waves are too weak to reach any detector that far away
Part of the core is liquid: S-waves cannot pass through liquid

items.why: The specification states that S-waves cannot travel through a liquid. Their absence on the far side, while P-waves still arrive, is the evidence that part of the core is liquid.

items.stem: A P-wave travels through solid rock. How does the rock itself move as the wave passes through it?

options.text: The rock is carried bodily along with the wave as it travels
The rock moves from side to side across the direction of travel
The rock vibrates back and forth in the direction of travel
The rock stays perfectly still while the wave passes

items.why: P-waves are longitudinal, so the oscillations of the rock are parallel to the direction in which the wave travels. The rock returns to its position; only energy moves on.

items.stem: Survey waves pass easily through rock layer X but are strongly absorbed by rock layer Y. How does this difference help the team explore ground they cannot see?

options.text: A weak returning signal shows the waves went through layer Y
Strong absorption sends back a stronger reflection from layer Y
Layer Y reflects every wave, so nothing returns from below
Both layers return the same signal, so absorption is no use

items.why: How much a signal has been weakened is itself information. Waves that come back weak have passed through the strongly absorbing rock, so the strength of each returning signal maps out where each type of rock lies.

items.stem: Echo sounding uses high frequency sound waves rather than light or radio waves. Why is sound the wave that is used?

options.text: Sound travels faster through deep sea water than light does
Water absorbs light and radio waves in a short distance
Any wave would work here; sound is just the usual choice
Sound is the only wave the sea bed can reflect back

items.why: This is the use of absorption the specification asks students to explain. Light and radio waves do not survive the journey to the sea bed and back; high frequency sound does, so it can carry the information.

items.stem: P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids. How does this provide evidence about the Earth's core?

options.text: Where their speed changes shows where the core begins and ends
P-waves keep one fixed speed, so arrival times give distance only
P-waves are absorbed by the core, so a shadow shows its size
P-waves cannot enter the core, so nothing arrives beyond it

items.why: A change of speed marks a change of material. Tracking where P-waves speed up or slow down, and where they arrive, gives evidence for both the structure and the size of the core.

items.stem: The study of seismic waves led to discoveries about parts of the Earth which are not directly observable. What did the seismic waves provide?

options.text: Confirmation of what deep drilling had already shown
Evidence about material that nobody has seen
Ideas about the deep Earth that can never be tested
A direct view of the core through the rock above

items.why: The waves pass through regions no one can observe and carry information back out. That indirect evidence is what led to the discoveries about the Earth's interior.
